subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Ideal gases
themeLabel: Models of the particulate nature of matter
bigPicture: An ideal gas is a model: point particles that never attract each other and bounce perfectly. Real gases come close at high temperature and low pressure, and the model gives one simple equation, PV = nRT, linking pressure, volume, temperature and amount.

keyIdeas.cue: What does the ideal gas model assume?
keyIdeas.answer: Particles in constant random motion; their own volume is negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular forces; collisions are perfectly elastic (no loss of kinetic energy).

keyIdeas.cue: When and why do real gases deviate?
keyIdeas.answer: At low temperature, particles move slowly so attractions matter; at high pressure, particles are crowded so their own volume is no longer negligible. Deviation is greatest for polar or large molecules. No maths needed.

keyIdeas.cue: How do P, V and T relate for a fixed amount of gas?
keyIdeas.answer: At constant T, V ∝ 1/P (a curve; V against 1/P is a straight line). At constant P, V ∝ T in kelvin (a straight line through the origin at 0 K). At constant V, P ∝ T. Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa) = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹. Law names are not assessed.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you use PV = nRT and the combined gas law?
keyIdeas.answer: PV = nRT in SI units: P in Pa, V in m³, T in K, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Conversions: kPa × 1000; dm³ ÷ 1000; cm³ × 10⁻⁶. For a fixed amount changing conditions: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Rearrange to M = mRT/(PV) to find molar mass.

keyIdeas.cue: What causes gas pressure, and how do you explain the gas laws with it?
keyIdeas.answer: Pressure is the force from particles colliding with the container walls per unit area. Heat the gas: faster particles hit the walls more often and harder, so pressure rises (fixed V). Halve the volume: twice as many collisions per second per area.

keyIdeas.cue: How can you estimate absolute zero in the lab?
keyIdeas.answer: Measure the volume (or pressure) of a fixed amount of gas at several temperatures in °C, plot a straight line and extrapolate to zero volume/pressure. The estimate is rough: real gases liquefy long before, and the extrapolation is far beyond the data.

keyTerms.def: Model gas obeying PV = nRT exactly: no forces, negligible particle volume.
Collision with no loss of total kinetic energy.
Volume of one mole of gas; 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ for an ideal gas at STP.

workedExamples.title: Molar mass from gas data
workedExamples.prompt: 0.500 g of a gas occupies 300 cm³ at 25 °C and 101 kPa. Find its molar mass.
steps: SI units: V = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³; P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; T = 298 K.

workedExamples.title: Combined gas law
workedExamples.prompt: A balloon holds 2.00 dm³ at 20 °C and 100 kPa. Find its volume at −10 °C and 80.0 kPa.
steps: Units of P and V only need to match on both sides here; T must be in K.

misconceptions.wrong: Doubling the Celsius temperature doubles the volume.
misconceptions.right: Only a doubling of the kelvin temperature does that.

misconceptions.wrong: Any units work in PV = nRT.
misconceptions.right: With R = 8.31, use Pa and m³. kPa with dm³ also works (the factors of 1000 cancel), but mixing kPa and m³ does not.

misconceptions.wrong: Real gases deviate most at high temperature.
misconceptions.right: They deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

misconceptions.wrong: Real gases deviate because particles get bigger at high pressure.
misconceptions.right: Particle volume becomes a larger share of the space, and attractions pull particles back from the walls so they hit with less force; the most ideal gases are small and non-polar (e.g. He), the least ideal are polar (e.g. NH₃).

paper1B.data: Pressure–volume data for a gas at constant temperature: P/kPa 50, 100, 200, 400; V/cm³ 96, 48, 24, 12.
paper1B.prompt: Show the data fit the ideal model and state the graph that gives a straight line.
paper1B.answer: P × V = 4800 kPa cm³ every time, so V ∝ 1/P; plotting V against 1/P gives a straight line through the origin.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Unit conversion is the main mark-loser: Pa, m³, K. Write the converted values before substituting.
Use 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ (100 kPa STP), not the older 22.4.
Check whether a graph uses °C or K before deciding whether it should pass through the origin.
